core_summary: This environmental science chapter examines ecosystem structure, biotic and abiotic component interactions, food chains, and complex food webs. It analyzes energy flow efficiency following Lindeman's 10% law across trophic levels and the environmental accumulation of non-biodegradable toxins via biological magnification. Finally, it addresses major human impacts, specifically stratospheric ozone depletion driven by Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and municipal waste management strategies for biodegradable versus non-biodegradable garbage.
key_concepts: Ecosystem definition: Structural and functional unit comprising interacting biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic (temperature, water, soil, minerals) components
Natural ecosystems (forests, oceans, lakes) versus human-made artificial ecosystems (gardens, aquariums, crop fields)
Functional roles: Producers (photosynthetic plants/algae), Consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores, parasites), and Decomposers (bacteria, fungi recycling inorganic nutrients)
Food Chains and Food Webs: Linear feeding pathways versus interconnected complex networks
Unidirectional Energy Flow: Solar energy fixed by green plants (~1%) moves progressively through trophic levels
Lindeman's 10% Energy Law: Only ~10% of energy stored as organic matter at one trophic level is transferred to the next higher level; 90% lost to metabolic work and heat
Trophic level limitations: Energy loss restricts food chain length to 3-4 steps max
Biological Magnification: Progressive increase in concentration of non-biodegradable toxic chemicals (e.g. pesticides) at higher trophic levels, accumulating maximally in top apex consumers (humans)
Stratospheric Ozone (O3) Layer: Formation by solar UV action on oxygen (O2 -> O + O; O + O2 -> O3); Protective shielding against harmful UV-B rays causing skin cancer and cataracts
Ozone Depletion: Destruction of ozone molecules by Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used in refrigeration; 1987 UNEP Montreal Protocol freezing CFC production
Waste Disposal Management: Biodegradable wastes broken down naturally by biological saprophytic action versus Non-biodegradable wastes (plastics, synthetic chemicals) persisting indefinitely

key_terms.definition: A self-sustaining biological system formed by the interaction of living organisms with their non-living physical environment.
The living organisms of an ecosystem, including producers, consumers, and decomposers.
The non-living physical and chemical factors of an ecosystem such as temperature, sunlight, rainfall, soil, and minerals.
Autotrophic organisms (green plants and cyanobacteria) that produce organic food from inorganic substances using solar energy.
Heterotrophic organisms that obtain energy by consuming other organisms or organic matter.
Microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) that break down complex organic matter from dead organisms into simple inorganic nutrients.
Each distinct feeding step or energy level in a food chain.
A complex network of interconnected food chains reflecting natural feeding relationships within an ecosystem.
Ecological rule stating that on average only 10% of energy at a given trophic level is converted into biomass and transferred to the next level.
The progressive accumulation and increasing concentration of non-biodegradable toxic substances in organisms at higher trophic levels.
A atmospheric gas layer in the stratosphere containing high concentrations of O3 that shields Earth from harmful solar ultraviolet radiation.
Synthetic chemical compounds containing carbon, chlorine, and fluorine that catalyze the destruction of stratospheric ozone.
Waste materials that can be broken down into simpler non-toxic substances by natural biological decomposers.
Waste materials (such as plastics and heavy metals) that cannot be degraded by biological processes and persist in the environment.

key_takeaways: Decomposers are vital for nutrient recycling; without them, dead organic matter would pile up and soil fertility would collapse.
Energy flow in ecosystems is strictly unidirectional—solar energy captured by producers cannot revert back to the sun or lower levels.
Because of the 10% law, food chains rarely extend beyond 4 trophic levels due to massive cumulative thermal energy losses.
Non-biodegradable pesticides accumulate in highest concentrations in top carnivores and humans through biological magnification.
Global international agreements like the UNEP 1987 Montreal Protocol successfully halted CFC production to allow ozone layer recovery.
